source_text: Neque prius sanctissima Virgo donum admisit, quam, quis illud mitteret, et quodnam donum esset, ac quis ferret, addidicisset. Quae, dum secum, velut anceps loqueretur, ait ad Angelum: Unde sic nobis benedictionem apportasti? Ex cuiusmodi thesauris, verbi margarita nobis emissa est? Unde nobis donum materiam paravit? Ex caelo advenisti, at in terra incedis: humanam formam exhibes, et lucis fulgore resplendes.
thought_title: Mary questions the gift before accepting it
orientation: Mary speaks to Gabriel in the Annunciation dialogue, asking where his blessing comes from before she receives it.
pass_a_gloss: And the most holy Virgin did not admit the gift before she had learned who was sending it, and what sort of gift it was, and who was bearing it. She, while she was speaking with herself, as if hesitating, said to the Angel: From where have you thus brought blessing to us? From what sort of treasures has the pearl of the word been sent out to us? From where has the gift prepared matter for us? You have come from heaven, but you walk on earth: you display a human form, and you shine with the brightness of light.

choices.english: did not admit ... before she had learned
choices.why: keeps the negative temporal clause and past perfect force of learning before receiving
rejected: did not receive until she knew

choices.why: keeps the simile marker velut and the sense of divided speech here
literal genitive construction without forming a hyphenated compound
keeps ablative of means and genitive of source in plain words

pass_b_english: The most holy Virgin did not accept the gift before she had learned who sent it, and what the gift was, and who bore it. She weighed the matter within herself, and spoke as if hesitating, and said to the angel: "From where have you brought us this blessing in this way? From what kind of storehouse has this pearl of the word been sent out to us? From where has the gift drawn its substance for us? You have come from heaven, yet you walk upon the earth. You wear a human form, yet you shine with the brightness of light."

problems.quote: From where has it drawn the substance of this gift for us?
problems.why: In Latin, 'donum' is the nominative subject of 'paravit', not a genitive; English invents an 'it' as subject and makes 'this gift' modify 'substance'.
problems.fix: From where has the gift drawn its substance for us?
